```{r}
library(nflfastR)
library(nflreadr)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
```

```{r}
# make the contract first
nflcontracts <- load_contracts (file_type = getOption ("nflreadr.prefer", default = "rds")) 

# change variables in contracts dataset to clearly mark the start and end of a player's contract
nflcontracts <- nflcontracts %>% mutate(season_start = year_signed, season_end= (year_signed + years - 1))

# filter for years 2015 to 2023 for contracts
contracts_filtered <- nflcontracts %>% filter(season_start >= 2015, season_end <= 2023)

# load the player stats data from nflreadr in case we want to do all positions
playerstats <- load_player_stats (
  seasons = 2015:2023,
  stat_type = c("offense", "defense", "kicking"),
  file_type = getOption ("nflreadr.prefer", default = "rds")
) 

# filter and use the only offense dataset for now
offense_stats <- playerstats %>% filter(position %in% c("QB", "RB", "WR", "TE", "FB", "HB"))

# just a lil playing around to understand the two datasets
dim(contracts_filtered)
names(contracts_filtered)

dim(offense_stats)
names(offense_stats)

# from this line below I found that the stats dataset's season variable is just the year
sort(unique(offense_stats$season))
sort(unique(offense_stats$week))

# there is a chance gsis_id and player_id match

# Check overlap of IDs
contract_ids <- unique(contracts_filtered$gsis_id)
stats_ids <- unique(offense_stats$player_id)

length(intersect(contract_ids, stats_ids))           # overlap count
length(setdiff(contract_ids, stats_ids))             # only in contracts
length(setdiff(stats_ids, contract_ids))             # only in stats

# there are 1342 values of IDs that overlap, with around 5700 values that don't overlap. I'm going to make sure now that the ids actually refer to the same people

common_ids <- intersect(contracts_filtered$gsis_id, offense_stats$player_id)

# From contracts
contracts_check <- contracts_filtered %>%
  filter(gsis_id %in% common_ids) %>%
  select(gsis_id, contract_name = player) %>%
  distinct()

# From stats
stats_check <- offense_stats %>%
  filter(player_id %in% common_ids) %>%
  select(player_id, stats_name = player_display_name) %>%
  distinct()

# Combine for comparison
name_check <- inner_join(contracts_check, stats_check, by = c("gsis_id" = "player_id"))

# View sample
head(name_check, 40)

# this seems to track since the names are the exact same
```

```{r}
# I'm going to check now for name mismatches in combining the entirety of both datasets and use distinct() temporarily to not show any duplications

# Keep only one row per player in each dataset
contracts_names <- contracts_filtered %>%
  select(gsis_id, contract_name = player) %>%
  distinct(gsis_id, .keep_all = TRUE)

stats_names <- offense_stats %>%
  select(player_id, stats_name = player_display_name) %>%
  distinct(player_id, .keep_all = TRUE)

# Now join and check for name mismatches
name_check_all <- inner_join(
  contracts_names,
  stats_names,
  by = c("gsis_id" = "player_id")
)

# Check mismatches
name_mismatches <- name_check_all %>%
  filter(contract_name != stats_name)

nrow(name_mismatches)
name_mismatches

# this above shows that they are actually all the same person, but their names are spelled differently. This means that I can completely merge based on gsis_id = player_id. There's no need to clean names or join on them, since they don't represent any actual mismatches.

```
```{r}
#combine the data sets
# I realized we can't use an inner join because they aren't temporally aligned,
# so I'm using a filter (but not sure if it works properly)
# basically, I want to make sure that if a player has a contract that starts in 2022, the player doesn't take info from his 2019 season when he was under another contract

df_combined <- inner_join(
  contracts_filtered,
  offense_stats,
  by = c("gsis_id" = "player_id"),
  relationship = "many-to-many"
) %>%
  filter(season >= season_start, season <= season_end)

# lastly, I'm gonna add a variable that flags whether a row of stats is about their contract year performance or not

df_combined <- df_combined %>% mutate(contract_year = (season == season_end))

dim(df_combined)
head(df_combined)

# shows that there are 1250 unique players within this dataset
length(unique(df_combined$player))

```

```{r}
# I think next steps would be:
## double checking and going through the combined dataset that it all makes sense    the way that I combined it
## cleaning the combined dataset further by picking the variables that we need
    ## looking at head(df_combined), there's a ton of cols that we don't need,           such as the urls, college, height, weight, years, etc

# we decided that our final dataset did not need any of the following columns listed in the select function below
  ## these columns are either not useful in analysis of player performance or redundant variables

df_combined_clean <- df_combined %>% select(
    -target_share,
    -date_of_birth,
    -player_page,
    -height,
    -weight,
    -college,
    -cols,
    -headshot_url,
    -player_display_name,
    -opponent_team,
    -draft_year,
    -draft_round,
    -draft_overall,
    -draft_team,
    -is_active,
    -value,
    -otc_id,
    -season_start,
    -season_end,
    -player_name,
    -player_display_name,
    -position.y,
    -season_type,
    -fantasy_points,
    -fantasy_points_ppr,
    -recent_team
  )

# I also want to rename some variables of the cleaned dataset as to make understanding easier

df_combined_clean <- df_combined_clean %>% rename(position = position.x)
df_combined_clean <- df_combined_clean %>% rename(contract_length = years)
df_combined_clean <- df_combined_clean %>% rename(player_id = gsis_id)


# I noticed that these are similar, but position_group is more high level, while position is more granular
unique(df_combined_clean$position_group)
unique(df_combined_clean$position)

str(df_combined_clean)
dim(df_combined_clean)

# This shows that the data set is actually almost split half half between contract and non contract years
sum(df_combined_clean$contract_year==TRUE)
sum(df_combined_clean$contract_year==FALSE)
```

```{r}
# I want to make a couple more variables that will help us better analyze player performances 

# first, we are adding a total_epa variable that represents the epa within all categories (passing, receiving, and rushing)
  # each game has a different epa for the player, and depending on position the player might have NA values in epas within sections that don't apply to them. 
  # therefore, we must remove all na values when calculating this value
df_combined_clean <- df_combined_clean %>% mutate(total_epa = rowSums(select(., ends_with("_epa")), na.rm = TRUE))

# we are adding a completion % variable, which is helpful for performance analysis on QBs. Completion % = (completions/attempts)
df_combined_clean <- df_combined_clean %>% mutate(completion_percent = ifelse(!is.na(attempts) & attempts > 0, (completions/attempts)*100, NA))

# we are also adding yards per carry, which is helpful for analysis of RB positions, as well as QB when they run the ball. yards_per_carry = rushing_yards / carries
df_combined_clean <- df_combined_clean %>% mutate(yards_per_carry = ifelse(!is.na(carries) & carries > 0, rushing_yards/carries, NA))

# last, we are adding catch rate, which is helpful for performance analysis of WR positions. catch_rate = receptions/targets
df_combined_clean <- df_combined_clean %>% mutate(catch_rate = ifelse(!is.na(targets) & targets > 0, (receptions/targets)*100, NA))

dim(df_combined_clean)
head(df_combined_clean)

```
# Analyzing the value of running backs
```{r}
df_combined_clean %>%
  filter(position == "RB") %>%
  group_by(contract_year) %>%
  summarize(avg_epa = mean(total_epa, na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = contract_year, y = avg_epa, fill = contract_year)) + geom_col() + labs(x = "Contract Year", y = "Average EPA per Game")
```

Suggests that for running backs, on average, players do equally as bad in
their contract year compared to other years. Another point this brings up is
that running backs, when measured by their epa, are a detriment to their
team's performance. However, this is an exaggeration and maybe a
misinterpretation of the data because if they were a detriment to team
success, why would they be paid so much, if at all? Let's see how much
running backs are paid when compared to other positions.

```{r}
df_combined_clean %>%
  group_by(position) %>%
  summarize(avg_apy = mean(apy)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = position, y = avg_apy, fill = position)) + geom_col() + labs(x = "Position", y = "Average APY per Game")
```

This shows that RBs are the 4th highest paid position on average. If they
have a negative average epa, then why are they paid so much? To answer this
question, we need to understand what in a football game rewards players with
higher epas. The epa stat is biased towards explosive plays over consistent,
small yardage gains. So, by nature, running backs tend to get a smaller epa
than other positions. If we want to visualize another variable that can show
this position's effectiveness on the field, we can look at the yards per
carry stat.

```{r}
df_combined_clean %>%
  filter(position == "RB") %>%
  group_by(contract_year) %>%
  summarize(avg_yd_per_carry = mean(rushing_yards / carries, na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = contract_year, y = avg_yd_per_carry, fill = contract_year)) + geom_col() + labs(x = "Contract Year", y = "Average Yards per Carry")
```

This visualization shows that running backs, whether in their contract year
or not, tend to have relatively consistent, positive yardage gains per
carry. This has not only have the benefit of getting the ball closer to
scoring points, but also wears out the opposing team's defense. Being able
to consistently come out of a play with positive gains adds value to the
position that epa might not capable of showing.

# Analyzing the performance of wide receivers in their contract year
```{r}
df_combined_clean %>%
  filter(position == "WR") %>%
  group_by(contract_year) %>%
  summarize(avg_rec_yds = mean(receiving_yards)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = contract_year, y = avg_rec_yds, fill = contract_year)) + geom_col() + labs(x = "Contract Year", y = "Average Receiving Yards per Game")
```

Suggests that wide receivers, on average, score fewer receiving yards per game during their contract year.

```{r}
df_combined_clean %>%
  filter(position == "WR") %>%
  group_by(contract_year) %>%
  summarize(avg_receptions = mean(receptions)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = contract_year, y = avg_receptions, fill = contract_year)) + geom_col() + labs(x = "Contract Year", y = "Average Receptions per Game")
```

Suggests that wide receivers, on average, have fewer receptions during their
contract year. Let's narrow this down to just a few high yardage wide
receivers.

```{r}
df_combined_clean %>%
  group_by(player) %>%
  filter(mean(receiving_yards, na.rm = TRUE) >= 65) %>%
  group_by(contract_year) %>%
  summarize(avg_receptions = mean(receptions)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = contract_year, y = avg_receptions, fill = contract_year)) + geom_col() + labs(x = "Contract Year", y = "Average Receptions per Game")
```

Now this closes the gap by a considerable margin. I chose to filter by
players who average 65 or more yards per game because this would set them at
65 yards/game * 17 games/season = 1105 yards per season, which is
considerably good for wide receivers. The increase in average receptions
during these star players' contract years leads us to believe that for star
wide receivers, the quarterback is about equally as likely to pass the ball
to them regardless of whether they are in their contract year or not. This
also brings up that the lower average receptions in wide receivers' contract
years is washed out by average or below average wide receivers. 

# Salary based on previous contract year epa
```{r}
epa_contract_year <- df_combined_clean %>%
  mutate(contract_year_year = year_signed + contract_length - 1) %>%
  filter(season == contract_year_year) %>%
  group_by(player, contract_year_year) %>%
  summarize(contract_year_epa = mean(total_epa, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")
next_contract <- df_combined_clean %>%
  select(player, year_signed, guaranteed, position) %>%
  rename(year_signed_next = year_signed, guaranteed_next = guaranteed)
df_combined_sal <- epa_contract_year %>%
  left_join(next_contract, by = c("player" = "player", "contract_year_year" = "year_signed_next"))
QB_model <- lm(guaranteed_next ~ contract_year_epa, data = df_combined_sal %>% filter(position == "QB"))
QB_slope <- coef(QB_model)[["contract_year_epa"]]
RB_model <- lm(guaranteed_next ~ contract_year_epa, data = df_combined_sal %>% filter(position == "RB"))
RB_slope <- coef(RB_model)[["contract_year_epa"]]
WR_model <- lm(guaranteed_next ~ contract_year_epa, data = df_combined_sal %>% filter(position == "WR"))
WR_slope <- coef(WR_model)[["contract_year_epa"]]
# QBs
df_combined_sal %>%
  filter(!is.na(guaranteed_next), position == "QB") %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = contract_year_epa, y = guaranteed_next)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, color = "blue") + 
  annotate("text", x = Inf, y = -Inf, hjust = 1.1, vjust = -1, label = paste0("Slope: ", round(QB_slope, 2)), size = 4, color = "black") +
  labs(x = "Contract Year EPA", y = "Guaranteed Money in Next Contract")
# RBs
df_combined_sal %>%
  filter(!is.na(guaranteed_next), position == "RB") %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = contract_year_epa, y = guaranteed_next)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, color = "blue") +
  annotate("text", x = Inf, y = -Inf, hjust = 1.1, vjust = -1, label = paste0("Slope: ", round(RB_slope, 2)), size = 4, color = "black") +
  labs(x = "Contract Year EPA", y = "Guaranteed Money in Next Contract")
# WRs
df_combined_sal %>%
  filter(!is.na(guaranteed_next), position == "WR") %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = contract_year_epa, y = guaranteed_next)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, color = "blue") +
  annotate("text", x = Inf, y = -Inf, hjust = 1.1, vjust = -1, label = paste0("Slope: ", round(WR_slope, 2)), size = 4, color = "black") +
  labs(x = "Contract Year EPA", y = "Guaranteed Money in Next Contract")
```
